segments.title: The Thaon di Revel class and its patrol designation
segments.body: The official designation is multipurpose offshore patrol vessel. Italy assigned the PPA work previously done by Soldati frigates and Minerva corvettes. The programme uses a large hull in Light, Light Plus and Full configurations. Those equipment levels give the navy different combat capabilities under the same patrol designation.

evidence.note: Patrol designation and predecessor classes.
Light, Light Plus and Full displacement comparison.

segments.summary: Italy's multipurpose offshore patrol vessel takes over frigate and corvette duties, with three equipment levels on a large common hull.

segments.title: The Soldati frigates and Minerva corvettes replaced by the PPA
segments.body: The PPA takes over roles previously filled by Soldati-class light patrol frigates and Minerva-class corvettes. Together, those predecessor classes account for twelve vessels in the replacement comparison. Italy's offshore patrol designation therefore covers duties inherited from both frigates and corvettes.

evidence.note: Replacement of the roles of twelve Soldati frigates and Minerva corvettes.

segments.summary: Italy's new patrol ship took on duties from the Soldati frigates and Minerva corvettes.

segments.title: How much lighter are the PPA Light and Light Plus?
segments.body: At full load, the quoted displacements are 6,270 tons for Full, 5,880 for Light Plus and 5,830 for Light. Light Plus saves 390 tons against Full, while Light saves 440 tons. Full and Light Plus are both close to 5,000 tons at light displacement, compared with 4,880 tons for Light. The larger differences at full load distinguish the variants more clearly than their light-displacement figures.

evidence.note: Full-load displacements of 6,270, 5,880 and 5,830 tons, with Light at 4,880 tons light displacement.

segments.summary: The Light, Light Plus and Full configurations differ more at full load than they do at light displacement.

segments.title: The PPA hull and combined diesel and gas propulsion
segments.body: The hull is about 143 metres overall and 133 metres between perpendiculars. A General Electric Avio LM2500+G4 gas turbine combines with two MTU main diesel engines in a CODAG arrangement, meaning combined diesel and gas. Four diesel generators and electric motors provide a low-speed propulsion option. Combined power gives a quoted top speed of 31.6 knots. This machinery supports the assessment that the PPA has frigate-like performance despite its patrol designation.

evidence.note: Approximate hull dimensions, LM2500+G4 turbine, two MTU main diesels, four diesel generators and electric motors. The captioned turbine power unit is unclear.
Speeds under combined, diesel and diesel-electric propulsion.

segments.summary: A hull of about 143 metres and several propulsion options explain why the PPA's performance draws comparisons with frigates.

segments.title: PPA speed under electric, diesel and combined power
segments.body: Combined diesel and gas power gives a quoted 31.6 knots. Both main diesels give 25 knots, while one gives 18 knots. Diesel-electric running provides 10 knots. These options combine slow patrol operation with substantially faster transit.

evidence.note: 31.6 knots under combined power, 25 on two diesels, 18 on one diesel and 10 under diesel-electric power.

segments.summary: The quoted speeds show how the ship's performance changes with the machinery it uses.

segments.title: PPA cruising range and room for embarked personnel
segments.body: The quoted cruising range is 5,000 nautical miles at 15 knots. Maximum personnel capacity reaches 200, including 30 in a module zone. Normal complements are smaller: 120 for Full and 90 for both Light Plus and Light. Extra accommodation allows a ship to embark personnel associated with its mission equipment as well as its usual crew.

evidence.note: 5,000 nautical miles at 15 knots, capacity for 200 including 30 in a module zone, and normal complements of 120 or 90.

segments.summary: A normal crew of 90 or 120 leaves room within the stated 200-person capacity for additional mission personnel.

segments.title: The case for calling the PPA a light frigate
segments.body: The PPA's patrol designation sits alongside the displacement and propulsion performance of a substantially equipped warship. The light-frigate assessment rests on those characteristics and the combat equipment the hull can carry. Full has a broader combat fit than the lighter configurations. A double hangar and stern ramp also support helicopter and boat operations. The classification is a judgement about the ship's capabilities, separate from Italy's official designation.

evidence.note: Light-frigate judgement despite the official patrol designation.
Combat fit by configuration, double hangar and stern ramp.

segments.summary: The classification argument brings together the ship's size, performance and the combat equipment that varies by version.

segments.title: The 127 mm and 76 mm guns in the PPA combat fit
segments.body: The gun arrangement places a 127 mm mount forward and a 76 mm mount aft. The missile fit described alongside them has sixteen cells for Aster 30 air-defence missiles. Equipment varies across the class, so this armament list cannot be applied to every ship. The lighter ships retain space for launch cells that have not necessarily been installed.

evidence.note: Forward 127 mm gun, aft 76 mm gun, sixteen Aster 30 cells and the subsequent caveat about uninstalled cells in lighter ships.

segments.summary: A 127 mm gun forward, a 76 mm gun aft and a sixteen-cell Aster 30 fit show the combat potential behind the patrol designation.

segments.title: What fitted for but not with means on a PPA
segments.body: The lighter ships retain hull space and design provision for missile-launch cells even when those cells are absent. Leaving the cells uninstalled accounts for part of their lower weight. The fuller armament described includes eight anti-ship missiles, while both Light and Light Plus have provision for those weapons without carrying them. Torpedoes also belong to the Full fit, with provision retained in the lighter ships. A shared hull therefore accommodates materially different combat fits at delivery.

evidence.note: Reserved launch-cell space, eight anti-ship missiles in the fuller fit, and Full-versus-light differences in torpedo installation.

segments.summary: The lighter fits illustrate how shipbuilders can leave room for later installation of combat equipment.

segments.title: Helicopters and boat facilities on the PPA
segments.body: The class can carry up to two helicopters, with personnel for the aviation detachment. A double hangar houses the helicopters, and a stern ramp handles rigid inflatable boats. The ramp can also accommodate other equipment. Helicopters and boats expand the area the ship can cover on patrol.

evidence.note: Embarked helicopter personnel and space for two helicopters.
Double hangar and a stern ramp for rigid inflatable boats.
Helicopters and boats extend patrol presence.

segments.summary: A double hangar and a stern ramp give the ship ways to extend its reach beyond the hull.

segments.title: PPA exports to Indonesia and Italy's move towards Full
segments.body: Indonesia bought ships from the programme while Italy continued building for its own fleet. The Italian procurement programme combines refitting existing ships to Full with building new ships in that configuration. These paths use the same design for export orders and for a more heavily equipped Italian fleet. The class's range of uses supports a recommendation to consider it in more ship competitions.

evidence.note: Indonesian sales and the account of Italian refits and new construction in the Full configuration.
Recommendation for wider consideration of the design in ship competitions.

segments.summary: Indonesia's purchase accompanies Italy's move towards Full through refits and new construction.

segments.title: What the proposed PPA Evo would add
segments.body: PPA Evo is a proposed development of the standard design. Its planned equipment includes uncrewed aircraft (UAVs) and uncrewed surface vessels (USVs). The quoted vertical-launch capacity is 64 cells. That larger missile fit supports assessing Evo as a frigate.

evidence.note: Proposed UAVs, USVs and 64 VLS cells. The third drone category is unclear in the captions.
Frigate assessment for the proposed Evo, distinct from the standard PPA's light-frigate classification.

segments.summary: The proposed PPA Evo combines uncrewed aircraft and surface vessels with 64 vertical-launch cells.

segments.title: How the PPA hull supports speed and mission flexibility
segments.body: The PPA hull was designed to support high-speed performance. The same hull provides adaptable spaces amidships and aft. These spaces can take equipment or containers according to the assignment. The design brings propulsion performance and mission flexibility together within one ship.

evidence.note: Hull design intended to support the quoted performance characteristics.
Amidships and aft spaces adaptable to the mission.

segments.summary: The PPA combines a hull designed for high performance with spaces that accept changing mission equipment.

segments.title: Where the PPA carries mission modules
segments.body: The PPA has one adaptable zone amidships and another aft. Containers and other systems can be placed in these spaces to suit the assignment. The intended advantage is a relatively quick change of mission equipment within the same hull. Leonardo electronics form part of the wider equipment fit.

evidence.note: Amidships and aft zones for relatively quick changes of containers or other mission equipment, and a Leonardo electronics fit.

segments.summary: The two adaptable zones have room for containers or equipment suited to a particular assignment.

segments.title: Where PPAs fit in a carrier or amphibious group
segments.body: A force made up entirely of standard PPAs is judged to have limited combat weight. A mixed task group can combine PPAs with frigates and air-warfare assets around a carrier or landing helicopter dock (LHD). In that setting, the PPAs add useful hulls to a formation with a broader range of capabilities. The proposed Evo is set aside in this comparison because its heavier fit supports a frigate classification.

evidence.note: Limited assessment of an all-PPA force, excluding Evo, compared with PPAs contributing to a carrier or LHD group with frigates and air-warfare assets.

segments.summary: Standard PPAs are assessed as useful additions to a force containing frigates, air-warfare ships and a carrier or amphibious ship.

segments.title: PPA presence in the Mediterranean and farther afield
segments.body: Mediterranean patrols among the islands are one use for the PPA. Operations in the Indian Ocean and a recent Italian deployment to Japan illustrate its reach beyond the region. Joining allied task groups gives the ship another role during such deployments. Its capabilities support the argument that it adds useful strength when a navy needs more hulls for presence and group operations.

evidence.note: Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, Japan and allied-group examples in the presence argument.

segments.summary: Mediterranean patrols, Indian Ocean operations and a deployment to Japan illustrate the PPA's value for presence and allied task groups.

segments.title: Why submarine detection matters to the PPA classification
segments.body: Active and passive towed sonar underpin the assessment of the PPA's anti-submarine capability. Submarine detection gives the design an escort role alongside its patrol duties. A patrol emphasis is compatible with serious attention to anti-submarine warfare, which is also a primary concern across the other ships under comparison. This gives the light-frigate assessment a basis beyond missile capacity.

evidence.note: Active and passive towed sonar and the assessment of anti-submarine capability. The precise sensor terminology and fit by variant remain unclear.
Patrol emphasis alongside anti-submarine capability, with ASW a primary concern across the ships under comparison.

segments.summary: Active and passive towed sonar support the case for a patrol-oriented ship with useful anti-submarine capability.

segments.title: Why the proposed PPA Evo is judged a frigate
segments.body: Light frigate is the assessment for the standard PPA, with its emphasis on patrol. That role still allows substantial anti-submarine capability. Evo's proposed increase in missile capacity would move the design into the frigate category in this classification. The judgement therefore distinguishes the existing configurations from the more heavily armed proposal.

evidence.note: Patrol emphasis and anti-submarine capability in the standard PPA, with more missiles shifting the proposed Evo towards a frigate classification.
Closing light-frigate judgement, with acknowledgement that others may classify the standard ship as a frigate.

segments.summary: Patrol duties support the light-frigate assessment of the standard PPA, while Evo's proposed larger missile fit supports a frigate classification.

segments.title: Why speed matters for Italian patrols in the Mediterranean
segments.body: A patrol ship can need to move quickly across the Mediterranean as events develop. High speed allows it to reposition between areas where its presence will be noticed. The proposed use is to make those passages quickly, then resume a visible patrol, creating the impression of a wider presence. Helicopters and rigid inflatable boats extend the area the ship can cover once it arrives. That combination makes the PPA's powerful machinery relevant to Italy's patrol requirements.

evidence.note: Fast repositioning between visible patrols across the Mediterranean, with helicopters and boats extending the ship's presence.

segments.summary: Fast transit lets a patrol ship move between Mediterranean stations and maintain a visible presence across a wider area.

segments.title: Why the PPA carries two naval gun calibres
segments.body: One personal preference is to replace the mixed gun fit with three 76 mm mounts. The PPA instead combines a 127 mm gun with a 76 mm gun. The larger weapon has a range of ammunition options that helps justify retaining it. Those options give a reason to accept the mixed battery even when a uniform 76 mm fit is attractive.

evidence.note: Personal preference for three 76 mm mounts, qualified by the ammunition options available to the 127 mm gun.

segments.summary: A personal preference for three 76 mm guns is weighed against the ammunition options offered by the PPA's 127 mm mount.

segments.title: From Vickers and Terni Steelworks to OTO Melara
segments.body: OTO Melara traces its origins to a joint venture between Vickers and Terni Steelworks. That connection gives Vickers a place in the ancestry of Italian naval guns still in use. OTO Melara produced both the 76 mm and 127 mm gun families discussed here. These weapons now appear under the Leonardo name.

evidence.note: Vickers and Terni Steelworks joint-venture origins, the 76 mm and 127 mm gun families, and the Leonardo connection. The subsequent Finmeccanica wording is unclear.

segments.summary: The two PPA gun calibres lead back to a joint venture between a British engineering company and an Italian steelmaker.
